passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel anti‑inflammatory compound, Compound X, on cytokine production in cultured murine macrophages. Cells were treated with 0, 10, 25, or 50 µM of Compound X for 24 hours, then the concentration of interleukin‑6 (IL‑6) in the supernatant was quantified by ELISA. The study aimed to determine whether Compound X could suppress IL‑6 release in a dose‑dependent manner. In addition to the treatment groups, a vehicle control (0.1% DMSO) was included to account for solvent effects. The experiment was performed in triplicate wells for each concentration. The researchers reported that IL‑6 production decreased progressively with increasing concentrations of Compound X, with the lowest level observed at 50 µM. No cytotoxicity was noted at any concentration, as cell viability remained above 90% across all groups. These findings suggest that Compound X may inhibit inflammatory signaling pathways in macrophages.

stem: Which concentration of Compound X resulted in the lowest IL‑6 production?
explanation: The table shows IL‑6 levels decreasing with higher concentrations; the lowest value (30 pg/mL) occurs at 50 µM.
trap: The distractor A (0 µM) represents the untreated baseline, which is higher, not lower.

stem: Which control condition best accounts for the potential effect of the solvent used to dissolve Compound X?

options.C: Cells treated with the lowest drug dose (10 µM)

explanation: Correct: B) A vehicle control gives cells the solvent without the drug, isolating any solvent effect. Why the others are wrong: A) Untreated cells receive no solvent, so they cannot reveal a solvent effect. C) A low drug dose contains drug as well as solvent, so effects cannot be separated. D) A high drug dose also contains drug, so it cannot isolate the solvent.
trap: Choosing untreated cells (option A) because they receive no drug; they also receive no solvent, so they cannot show a solvent effect.

stem: Calculate the percent reduction in IL‑6 production at 25 µM compared with the 0 µM control.
explanation: Percent reduction = (120 – 60)/120 × 100 = 50%. The other options misapply the formula or use incorrect values.
trap: Using the wrong base for percent reduction, such as dividing the 60 pg/mL drop by the treated value instead of the 0 µM control value of 120 pg/mL.

stem: Which statement is incorrect regarding the experimental results?

options.A: Compound X is cytotoxic at 50 µM.
options.B: IL‑6 levels decrease with increasing concentration of Compound X.
options.C: The experiment used triplicate wells for each concentration.
options.D: A vehicle control containing 0.1% DMSO was included.

explanation: Correct: A) The passage states cell viability remained above 90% at every concentration, so no cytotoxicity was noted. Why the others are wrong: B) The table shows IL-6 falling from 120 to 30 pg/mL as concentration rose. C) The passage states triplicate wells were used. D) The passage states a 0.1% DMSO vehicle control was included.
trap: Reading the falling IL-6 as a sign of cell death (option A); viability stayed above 90%, so the decrease is not explained by cytotoxicity.

stem: Which reported result argues against the possibility that the lower IL‑6 was simply due to dead cells?

options.A: Cell viability remained above 90% at every concentration.
options.B: IL‑6 fell progressively with increasing concentration.
options.C: Triplicate wells were used for each concentration.
options.D: A vehicle control (0.1% DMSO) was included.

explanation: Correct: A) High viability at all doses shows the cells were alive, so the lower IL-6 is not explained by cell death. Why the others are wrong: B) A dose-dependent fall in IL-6 is the effect being explained, not evidence against cell death. C) Replication improves precision but says nothing about viability. D) A vehicle control accounts for solvent effects, not cell death.
trap: Choosing the vehicle control (option D) because it is a control; it addresses solvent effects, whereas only the viability data address cell death.
